title: A Randomised Control Trial of Interleaved Mathematics Practice https://gwern.net/doc/psychology/spaced-repetition/2019-rohrer.pdf
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), November 21, 2024 — original paper:
summary: Barton summarises Rohrer and colleagues' large randomised controlled trial testing interleaved versus blocked maths practice across 54 seventh-grade classes over four months. Students who received a higher dose of interleaved assignments substantially outperformed those on mostly blocked practice on a delayed, unannounced test given a month later, 61% versus 38% correct. Barton highlights that the intervention required no special teacher training and was judged feasible by the participating teachers, even though interleaved assignments took students somewhat longer to complete than blocked ones. He draws out the practical recommendation that some initial blocked practice may still help when introducing a brand-new skill, but that interleaving should follow soon after, and that teachers can push publishers to build more interleaved material into textbooks and software, since it remains scarce.
points: Students given more interleaved maths practice scored 61% versus 38% for the mostly-blocked group on an unannounced test a month later — a substantial, unprompted retention gain.
Interleaved practice was feasible for ordinary teachers to implement without specific training, though it took students longer to complete than blocked assignments.
The benefits of interleaving were more pronounced with longer test delays, suggesting it's especially valuable for cumulative exams and long-term retention goals.
Some initial blocked practice may still help when a skill is brand new, before shifting into interleaved practice to build genuine discrimination between problem types.

Interleaved practice, which involves mixing different types of math problems within an assignment, can substantially improve students' performance on delayed tests.
Interleaved practice is a feasible intervention that teachers can implement without extensive training.
